plan.topic: Is low blood sugar why you feel tired on tirzepatide? How uncommon hypoglycemia was in SURMOUNT-1 (people without diabetes) vs the label's higher risk when combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea
plan.angle:
20:00 funnel Short (Exp D) and spin-off of L1. It asks one fresh question, about low blood sugar, rather than re-cutting L1 or repeating the 10-31 fatigue Short. 60–85 s, 170 words or fewer.

Answer within 10 s: 'Tired or shaky on tirzepatide? Low blood sugar is a common worry, but in the big obesity trial in people without diabetes it was uncommon.' Copy the per-arm hypoglycemia rates vs placebo exactly from NEJM 2022 SURMOUNT-1 or the label, with the population named. If they can't be confirmed, use the label's qualitative wording instead.

The new fact is the label's warning that the risk of low blood sugar is higher when tirzepatide is used with insulin or a sulfonylurea, so ask your prescriber. Give the low blood sugar signs in label wording. One line: other everyday causes of tiredness are covered in the full video.

Also required:
- 'Don't stop or change your medicines on your own.'
- One GI line.
- 'Not personal advice' and the prescriber line, both spoken and on screen.
- No Exp F line, no spoken titles.
- Last line: 'Full breakdown on our channel, link in the description.'

L1's URL goes on description line 1 only once it's verified live. Otherwise link Side Effects and don't count this Short toward Exp D. Mix at 0.02 or lower.

package.title: Is Tirzepatide Fatigue Actually Low Blood Sugar? #shorts
package.description:
Quick answer: in SURMOUNT-1 (no diabetes), very low readings were reported in 0.3% on tirzepatide vs 0% on placebo; the trial didn't routinely check for it. Risk may be higher with insulin or a sulfonylurea. Fatigue was reported in 5–7% on tirzepatide (by dose) vs 3% on placebo in the label's weight-loss trials.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation.

Sources:
- Jastreboff et al., NEJM 2022 (SURMOUNT-1), PMID 35658024
- Zepbound Prescribing Information, rev. 8/2026, Section 5.7 & 6.1
- Zepbound Medication Guide, 2026

social.facebook_caption:
If you're on tirzepatide and feeling tired or a little shaky, it's natural to wonder if your blood sugar dropped. Here's the honest answer: in SURMOUNT-1, which studied adults without diabetes, very low readings were reported in 0.3% of people on tirzepatide and 0% on placebo (the trial didn't routinely check for it). The label says the risk may be higher if you're also on insulin or a sulfonylurea, so that's worth a conversation with your prescriber.

Here's what the label does list: tiredness itself. In the label's weight-loss trials, fatigue was reported in 5–7% on tirzepatide (by dose) versus 3% on placebo. Fluids, eating less and sleep can all play a part too, so low blood sugar isn't the only suspect.

Low blood sugar signs may include dizziness, shakiness, sweating, hunger, confusion, headache or a fast heartbeat. If you get these signs, tell your prescriber. If they're severe, get medical help right away.

script.hook_pattern: Opens on a question the viewer recognises ("Tired or shaky on tirzepatide?") and validates the worry. Within 10 s it answers with the SURMOUNT-1 label figure: glucose below 54 mg/dL was reported in 0.3% on tirzepatide vs none on placebo, in adults without diabetes. It also says plainly that the trial didn't routinely check for it. Two re-hooks follow. "Here's the catch" brings in the label's higher-risk combinations (insulin or a sulfonylurea). "Here's what the label does list" brings in fatigue as a documented side effect (5–7% by dose vs 3% on placebo). It ends with relief and agency: other everyday causes, the safety lines and the funnel CTA.

factcheck.summary:
The science checks out and the piece can pass. I checked it against the Zepbound prescribing information (revised 8/2026).
- **Low blood sugar figure:** in Study 1 (SURMOUNT-1, adults with obesity or overweight and no type 2 diabetes), the label says "there was no systematic capturing of hypoglycemia, but plasma glucose <54 mg/dL was reported in 0.3% of ZEPBOUND-treated patients versus no placebo-treated patients." So "didn't routinely check for it" is a fair plain-English version.
- **Higher-risk combinations:** section 5.7 warns of higher risk with insulin or a sulfonylurea, so s3's wording is right.
- **Fatigue:** the label's Table 1 (Studies 1 and 2 pooled) gives 5%, 6% and 7% on the 5, 10 and 15 mg doses vs 3% on placebo, which matches "5–7% by dose vs 3%".
- **Signs list:** a search showed all 7 signs in the Medication Guide's low blood sugar section: dizziness, shakiness, sweating, hunger, confusion, headache and fast heartbeat. The PDF itself wouldn't open as text, so I didn't read them there directly.
- **Safety:** the "Not personal advice" line, the prescriber line, the don't-stop line and "get medical help right away" are all present. None of it is dosing or switching advice.
- **Citation:** SURMOUNT-1 is confirmed as Jastreboff et al., NEJM 2022 (PMID 35658024), from search results. The PubMed page itself wouldn't load.

Four minor fixes remain: the script is one word over the 170-word Shorts limit; the 0.3% figure is tagged to the NEJM paper, though I only confirmed it in the label; the narration doesn't say the 54 mg/dL cut-off that the on-screen text shows; and if this runs at 08:00 or 13:00 it needs the Exp F subscribe line.
